issues.legal_issue: A single fatal blow with a deadly weapon to a vital part of the body can constitute murder when the circumstances establish that the offender knew the act was so imminently dangerous that it would in all probability cause death, and the mere fact that the blow was single does not establish a sudden fight or exclude murder.
material_facts: Four eyewitnesses, including an injured witness, consistently testified that the respondent struck the deceased on the skull with an axe.
Medical evidence established that the sharp-edged weapon caused a fractured skull and that the injury caused the deceased’s death.
A blood-stained axe was recovered at the respondent’s instance.
The deceased was unarmed when he was seized and assaulted.
The record did not support the High Court’s inference that the incident arose without premeditation in a sudden fight.
issues.conclusion: The respondent’s act fell within Section 300 Fourthly of the Penal Code and constituted murder under Section 302. Exception 4 to Section 300 did not apply; the single-blow circumstance did not justify reducing the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 300 Fourthly of the Penal Code, an act is murder where the offender knows it to be so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death. Whether a single blow establishes the requisite intention or knowledge depends on the circumstances, including the weapon, the part of the body struck, the force and manner of the blow, and the surrounding events; a single blow does not by itself rule out murder (Mahesh Balmiki v State of M.P.; Hukam Chand v State of Haryana; Pulicherla Nagaraju v State of A.P.; Singapagu Anjaiah v State of A.P.; Som Raj v State of H.P.). Exception 4 to Section 300 requires all of the following: absence of premeditation, a sudden fight, the act occurring in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct. A sudden fight involves mutual provocation and blows, and the exception cannot be established merely by showing absence of premeditation (Dhirajbhai Gorakhbhai Nayak v State of Gujarat).

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_used_deadly_weapon and fatal_blow_struck_vital_part and evidence_establishes_imminently_dangerous_act and not evidence_establishes_sudden_mutual_fight

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision that reduced a murder conviction to a lesser homicide conviction.
predicates.accused_used_deadly_weapon: The accused used a weapon capable of causing death in the assault.
predicates.fatal_blow_struck_vital_part: The accused struck the victim on a vital part of the body, and that injury caused the victim’s death.
predicates.evidence_establishes_imminently_dangerou: The evidence about the weapon, injury, and manner of assault establishes that the accused knew the act was so dangerous that it would in all probability cause death or such bodily injury as was likely to cause death.
predicates.evidence_establishes_sudden_mutual_fight: The evidence establishes that the victim and offender engaged in a sudden fight involving mutual provocation or blows.

issues.definition: When a murder-conviction appeal concerns a fatal vital-part blow with a deadly weapon, the evidence establishes an imminently dangerous act, and it does not establish a sudden mutual fight, the murder conviction is restored.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court’s reduction of a murder conviction may be set aside when its finding of a sudden, unpremeditated incident rests on surmise and disregards material eyewitness and other evidence, resulting in a manifestly perverse decision and a risk of miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The State appealed the High Court’s decision reducing the respondent’s conviction for murder to a lesser homicide offence.
The High Court inferred that the fatal assault occurred on the spur of the moment without premeditation.

The inference was unsupported by the evidence and disregarded the consistent eyewitness accounts, the weapon used, the fatal injury to a vital part, the medical evidence, and the circumstances of the assault.
The respondent’s claim that the deceased initiated the incident by pelting stones had no evidentiary basis.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was manifestly perverse and contrary to the record. The Supreme Court set it aside, restored the trial court’s murder conviction, and allowed the State’s appeal.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court may interfere where a challenged judgment is manifestly perverse and contrary to the evidence, and intervention is warranted to prevent a complete failure or miscarriage of justice. A conclusion about the circumstances of an assault must be grounded in the record and cannot disregard material evidence.

rule.if: state_appeal_from_reduced_conviction and high_court_inferred_sudden_unpremeditated_assault and inference_unsupported_by_record and high_court_ignored_material_evidence

predicates.state_appeal_from_reduced_conviction: The proceeding is a State appeal from a High Court decision reducing a criminal conviction.
predicates.high_court_inferred_sudden_unpremeditate: The High Court concluded that the assault was sudden and unpremeditated.
predicates.inference_unsupported_by_record: The evidence in the record does not support the High Court’s conclusion about how the assault arose.
predicates.high_court_ignored_material_evidence: The High Court disregarded material eyewitness, medical, or other evidence relevant to the assault and the injury.

issues.definition: In a State appeal from a reduced conviction, if the High Court’s conclusion that the assault was sudden and unpremeditated lacks support in the record and ignores material evidence, the High Court judgment is set aside and the trial conviction is restored.
